newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Famed Belgian battlefield site makes its mark.
newsitem.headline: Famed Belgian battlefield site makes its mark.

text.p: Japanese rubbed shoulders with Norwegians, Finns with French, Irish with Indians. There were even Belgians, alongside Greeks, as this famed battlefield town celebrated its 200th anniversary.

With civic leaders of 10 of the 75 other Waterloos scattered about the globe present, the original set about showing just how cosmopolitan it has become since the epic battle on June 18, 1815, when allied troops led by the Duke of Wellington broke French military dominance of Europe.
"We can learn from you and you from us. That is what the European Union is about," said the announcer for a group of Finnish folk dancers.
Many of the copy Waterloos were founded by soldiers who fought in the battle that changed the political face of Europe. On Saturday it was more a question of eating, drinking and listening.

Folk dance and song groups from France, Greece, Finland, Ireland, South Korea and others, took the stage as hundreds of people took advantage of the mild weather to sample the wares of the 12 nationalities offering food and drink.
Waterloo was founded as an independent commune in 1796 and is francophone -- many of the Belgian soldiers who fought on that fateful June day favoured Napoleon.

Nowadays, Waterloo has just over 28,000 inhabitants of whom nearly 5,500 are foreigners from an impressive total of 96 different countries -- giving some substance to the commune's claim to be among the most cosmopolitan in Belgium.
The central church has two corners full of plaques commemorating some of the 40,000 French and allied troops killed in the battle.
A casual visitor to the battlefield itself might be forgiven for thinking that maybe the Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte, revered as the greatest general of the age, won after all.
Ignoring the famed Lion Mound built to commemorate the death of the Prince of Orange during the battle, the tenor of the place is determinedly French.
